messages.content: Can you retrieve the weather forecast for White Plains for next week with temperatures in Celsius?

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.reasoning:
We need to call the function requests_get with appropriate parameters. The user wants weather forecast for White Plains for next week with temperatures in Celsius. We need to find latitude and longitude for White Plains. White Plains is a city in New York, USA. Coordinates roughly: 41.0535° N, 73.7629° W. So latitude=41.0535, longitude=-73.7629. We want forecast for next week. The Open-Meteo API supports daily forecasts. We can request daily parameters like temperature_2m_max, temperature_2m_min. Also we can specify timezone. For next week, we might want daily forecast for the next 7 days. The API allows "forecast_days" parameter? Actually, the Open-Meteo API has "daily" parameters and "start_date" and "end_date". We can set start_date to today and end_date to 7 days later. But we don't have date. We can use today's date. Let's assume we can get today's date via python datetime. But we can't run code. We can approximate. Today is 2026-07-20. Next week would be 2026-07-21 to 2026-07-27. So we can set start_date=2026-07-21, end_date=2026-07-27. Or we can just ask for daily forecast for next 7 days. The API may return daily forecast for next 7 days by default if not specified. But we can specify "forecast_days=7". Let's check the Open-Meteo API docs. The "daily" endpoint returns daily forecast for the next 7 days by default. So we can just request daily parameters.

We also need to set "temperature_unit=celsius" or "temperature_unit=metric"? The API uses "temperature_unit=metric" for Celsius. Actually, the Open-Meteo API uses "temperature_unit=metric" for Celsius. There's also "windspeed_unit=kmh" etc. So we can set "temperature_unit=metric".

Also we need "timezone=America/New_York" maybe.

So the request:

GET https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=41.0535&longitude=-73.7629&daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min&temperature_unit=metric&timezone=America/New_York

We can also add "start_date" and "end_date" but not necessary.
